newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: N.Korean defector group arrives after epic escape.
newsitem.headline: N.Korean defector group arrives after epic escape.

text.p: A family of 17, the biggest group of North Korean defectors since the Korean War, arrived in Seoul on Monday, six weeks after launching an epic escape through China and Hong Kong.
The band of men, women and young children included a security guard whose job was to stop just such defections through the wild and remote North Korea-China border.
Their escape was financed by relatives in the United States who sent money to pay guides to protect them in a month-long trek down the length of China which started on October 26.

In a saga that was the stuff of Hollywood films, the band passed from one safe house to another among two million ethnic Koreans in China, posing as a group of travelling rural labourers and even occasionally working in fields.
On November 23, they were smuggled into Hong Kong and freedom was then just Monday's three-hour flight away.
Tearful, smiling and bewildered, the family's journey ended at Kimpo Airport in Seoul in the light of a cold, grey dusk.
Kim Kyong-ho, the 62-year-old patriarch of the group, exclaimed to the South Korean brother he had not seen since the height of the 1950-53 Korean War: "Older Brother."

Kim Kyong-tae, 70, said the last time the pair were together was when they were separated in the war. The younger Kim, now missing half his left index finger, ended up in North Korea in the confusion at the end of the bloody conflict and said he was persecuted there for his South Korean roots.

"I didn't know if he was dead or alive. I'd heard rumours he was in the U.S. But when I saw pictures of the family after reports of their defection came out, his photo looked so much like me that I knew that it was him," the elder Kim said.
During their brief reunion, both brothers, overcome with emotion, at times had to rest in wheelchairs.

Surrounded by his wife, five sons and daughters, one seven-months pregnant, their wives and husbands, five grandchildren, and the border guard cousin who made the escape possible across the frozen Tuman river, Kim told reporters:
"I'm full of emotion that all my family has made it safely. We thank you countrymen for your warm welcome to our family."

The only person missing was Choi Yong-do, the 79-year-old father of Kim's wife Choi Hyon-sil, 57. From his home in New York he organised the money that allowed the group to bribe their way through four provinces of China and into Hong Kong.

Protected by 1,000 riot police and mobbed by journalists, the seven men, five women and five young children, loaded down with flowers from Seoul relatives, boarded a bus for a half-way house where intelligence agents waited to question them.

The escape was a propaganda coup for South Korea but also set off nervous speculation about how Seoul would cope if the defection was the start of a refugee surge from impoverished North Korea where floods have caused a year-long famine.
On the eve of the group's departure from Hong Kong, South Korean media reports said two other North Koreans were also in the British colony waiting their turn for asylum in Seoul.

An uncontrolled refugee exodus, signalling a breakdown of internal controls -- similar to the German experience -- is part of a nightmare scenario for Seoul, which would be left to pick up the pieces at a cost of billions of dollars.

South Korea will offer the family asylum and money modest by South Korean standards but a near-fortune in Stalinist North Korea. Seoul media speculated each person will receive about 10 million won ($12,000) to help settle and find work.

The sudden spate of refugees has put an unwelcome spotlight on Hong Kong as an escape centre for North Koreans just as the British colony enters the final months of its handover to China, one of Pyongyang's few allies.
"These cases are not the sort of problem they (British authorities in Hong Kong) need when they're tidying up the house," one Western diplomat said. "Its an awkward problem."
